summary: This document defines an RTCP Extended Report block for reporting a simple discard count metric, for use in a range of RTP applications.

plainLanguage.summary: When a media stream arrives with problems, the receiver has three possible fates for each packet: it is played, it is thrown away because it arrived too early or too late, or it never arrives at all. This RFC adds a small report to the periodic quality reports, so that the sender and the network operator can be told how many packets were thrown away and why. That separates a problem with the network from a problem with the sender's timing.

questions: what is rtcp xr discard count
what is a discarded rtp packet
difference between lost and discarded packets
subtitle: A small RTCP report block that tells a sender how many packets arrived fine but were never played.

tldr.problem: A receiver cannot always tell whether a packet that is missing from a media stream was lost in the network or arrived and was thrown away. The second case matters, because a packet that arrives too late to be played out is a transport problem the sender may be able to fix.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an RTCP Extended Report block, block type 24, that carries the number of packets discarded at the receiver, split by reason: a duplicate, a packet that arrived too early, and a packet that arrived too late. The block also says whether the count covers one reporting interval or the whole accumulation period.
tldr.outcome: Senders and network managers can see how much of the stream was thrown away and why, and can adjust their sending or the network before users notice. Used with the burst and gap discard block of RFC 7003, the two allow summary rates such as the gap discard rate to be calculated.

today: RFC 7002 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2013, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It registers block type 24 in the RTCP XR block type registry and the pkt-discard-count parameter in the RTCP XR SDP parameters registry.

sections.title: What the Block Counts
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new block type to augment those defined in RFC 3611, for use in a range of RTP applications. The new block type supports the reporting of the number of packets that are received correctly but are never played out, typically because they arrive too late, which the RFC calls buffer underflow, or too early, which it calls buffer overflow. The metric applies both to systems that use packet loss repair techniques such as forward error correction (RFC 5109) or retransmission (RFC 4588), and to those that do not.

The metric is useful for identifying the existence of packet transport problems, and for characterising their severity, where they may affect users' perceptions of a service delivered over RTP.

The block may be used together with the burst and gap discard block of RFC 7003, which reports the pattern of discarded packets. When both are sent to the media sender or to an RTP-based network management system, the information in the two allows the receiving system to calculate burst and gap summary statistics such as the gap discard rate. The metric in RFC 7003 can also be used on its own. The metric belongs to the class of transport-related end-system metrics defined in RFC 6792.

RTCP reporting is defined in RFC 3550, and RFC 3611 defined the extensible structure for reporting using an RTCP Extended Report (XR), which is the structure this new block is added to. The block follows the guidance on defining performance metrics in RFC 6390 and on reporting block formats in RFC 6792.
sections.plainLanguage:
This block counts the packets that arrived safely but were then thrown away instead of being played. That happens when a packet arrives so late that its moment has passed, or so early that the receiver has no room for it.

The count is worth reporting because it separates a timing problem from a loss problem. A packet that never arrived is one thing; a packet that arrived and was dropped is another, and the sender can often do something about the second. A companion block, defined in RFC 7003, adds the pattern of the drops, and the two together let the receiver work out summary rates such as the gap discard rate.

sections.title: Received, Lost and Discarded
sections.content:
The RFC uses three terms for the fate of a packet. A packet is regarded as lost if it fails to arrive within an implementation-specific time window. A packet that arrives within that window but is either too early or too late to be played out, or is thrown away before playout because of packet duplication or redundancy, is regarded as discarded. A packet is not regarded as discarded if it arrives within the window but is dropped during decoding by a higher layer decoder, for example because of a decoding error.

Every packet falls into exactly one of three classes: received, which the RFC also calls OK, discarded, or lost. The discard count metric counts only discarded packets. The metric for the cumulative number of packets lost, defined in RFC 3550, reports packets lost from the media stream, a single synchronization source within a single RTP session. The metric for the number of packets discarded reports the packets discarded from the media stream arriving at the receiver, again for a single synchronization source within a single RTP session. A further metric defined in RFC 5725 is available to report on packets that no repair technique recovers.
sections.plainLanguage:
Three words matter here. A packet is lost if it does not arrive within a time window the implementation chooses. A packet is discarded if it arrives in time but is still thrown away, because it arrived too early, too late, or was a duplicate. A packet that arrives and is then dropped by a decoder is neither, because nothing was lost and nothing was thrown away by the transport.

Every packet is exactly one of received, discarded or lost. This block counts only the discarded ones.

sections.title: The Block Layout
sections.content:
The metrics in the block report on the number of packets discarded in the stream arriving at the RTP end system, and the measurement is made at the receiving end. Instances of the block use the SSRC to refer to the separate auxiliary Measurement Information Block of RFC 6776, which describes the measurement periods in use. The block relies on the measurement interval in that block to indicate the span of the report, and it MUST be sent in the same compound RTCP packet as it. If the measurement interval is not received in the same compound RTCP packet, the metrics block MUST be discarded.

The block itself has a fixed layout of three 32-bit words. The first word holds the block type, the interval metric flag, the discard type and the reserved bits, followed by the block length. The second word holds the SSRC of the source, as defined in Section 4.1 of RFC 3611. The third word holds the discard count itself.
sections.plainLanguage:
The count is measured at the receiving end of the stream. The report has to be sent together with the separate block that says which time period the report covers, and in the same packet. If that second block is missing, the receiver is told to throw the count away, because a count without a period has no meaning.

The block itself is three words long: a header word, a word naming the stream the count belongs to, and the count.

sections.title: The Fields and Their Values
sections.content:
The block type is 8 bits and identifies the block with the constant 24. The interval metric flag is 2 bits and says whether the reported value covers the most recent measurement interval, I=10, the accumulation period of a cumulative measurement, I=11, or is a sampled instantaneous value, I=01. The discard count can only be measured over definite intervals and cannot be sampled, so the sampled value MUST NOT be sent and MUST be discarded when received, and the reserved value I=00 MUST NOT be sent and MUST be discarded when received.

The discard type is 2 bits and identifies why the packets were discarded: 00 for a packet discarded or being thrown away before playout because of packet duplication; 01 for a packet discarded because it was too early to be played out; and 10 for a packet discarded because it was too late to be played out. The value 11 is reserved for future definition, MUST NOT be sent and MUST be discarded when received. An endpoint MAY report any combination of discard types in each reporting interval by including several Discard Count Metrics Blocks in a single RTCP XR packet. The RFC notes that some systems send duplicate RTP packets for robustness, which is NOT RECOMMENDED because it breaks RTCP packet statistics, and points to the duplication mechanism of [RTPDUP] as an alternative that does not break the statistics.

The reserved field is 4 bits. Senders MUST set them to zero and receivers ignore them. The block length is 16 bits and gives the length of the report block in 32-bit words minus one, in accordance with RFC 3611. It MUST be set to 2, and the block MUST be discarded if the length is set to any other value.

The discard count is the number of packets discarded over the period covered by the report, whether an interval or a cumulative period. The measured value is unsigned. If it exceeds 0xFFFFFFFD, the value 0xFFFFFFFE MUST be reported to indicate an over-range measurement, and if the measurement is unavailable, the value 0xFFFFFFFF MUST be reported. The number of packets expected over the period is not repeated in this block, because it can be worked out from the difference between a pair of extended sequence numbers in the Measurement Information Block.
sections.plainLanguage:
The header of the block says three things: how the count is measured, why the packets were dropped, and how long the block is. Only three reasons are defined: the packet was a duplicate, it was too early, or it was too late. A receiver that sees the fourth value, or a length other than the one defined, is told to ignore the block.

The count itself is a plain number. Two special values report trouble with the measurement: one means the number was too large to fit, the other that no measurement was available at all.

sections.title: Signalling the Block with SDP
sections.content:
RFC 3611 defines the use of the Session Description Protocol (RFC 4566) for signalling the use of XR blocks, although XR blocks MAY be used without any prior signalling, as described in Section 5 of that RFC.

This RFC extends the rtcp-xr SDP attribute of RFC 3611 with an additional value of xr-format to signal the use of the report block defined here. The ABNF is xr-format =/ xr-pdc-block and xr-pdc-block = "pkt-discard-count". Where SDP is used in an offer and answer context, the unilateral rtcp-xr attribute parameter usage defined in Section 5.2 of RFC 3611 applies.

IANA has assigned the block type value 24 in the RTCP XR Block Type Registry to the Discard Count Metrics Block, and the new parameter pkt-discard-count in the RTCP XR SDP Parameters Registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The block can be used without any negotiation at all. If the two ends do want to agree on it first, it is announced in the session description, in the same attribute that announces the other extended report blocks, with the value pkt-discard-count.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In some situations, returning very detailed error information, such as an over-range measurement or an unavailable measurement, using this report block can give an attacker insight into the security processing. Where this is a concern, the implementation should apply encryption and authentication to the report block. The RFC gives the example of the Audio-Visual Profile with Feedback profile together with the Secure RTP profile, as defined in RFC 3711, a combination specified as SAVPF in RFC 5124.

Beyond that, the RFC believes the block introduces no new security considerations beyond those described in RFC 3611. The block does not provide per-packet statistics, so the risk to confidentiality described in Section 7 of RFC 3611 does not apply.
sections.plainLanguage:
The only risk the document points at is that the two special values in the count, which report a failed measurement, could tell an attacker something about how the system is working. Where that matters, the report should be encrypted and authenticated, for example with the secure profile for RTP feedback.

Other than that, the block adds no new risk, because it reports a summary count rather than anything about individual packets.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: Interval metric flag: interval, cumulative or sampled.

fields.name: DT
fields.desc: Discard type: duplicate, too early or too late.

fields.name: resv
fields.desc: Reserved bits; senders set them to zero and receivers ignore them.

fields.name: Block Length
fields.desc: Length of the block in 32-bit words minus one.

fields.name: SSRC of Source
fields.desc: The synchronization source the count belongs to.

fields.name: Discard Count
fields.desc: Number of packets discarded over the period covered by the report.

viz.caption: THE DISCARD TYPES THE BLOCK CAN REPORT

items.label: Discarded as a duplicate
items.desc: The packet was discarded or being thrown away before playout because of packet duplication.

items.label: Discarded, too early
items.desc: The packet was discarded because it was too early to be played out.

items.label: Discarded, too late
items.desc: The packet was discarded because it was too late to be played out.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Reserved for future definition. It must not be sent, and a block carrying it must be discarded.

viz.caption: THE THREE FATES OF A PACKET

cells: The packet arrived in time and was played, or was dropped later by a decoder
The packet arrived in time but was thrown away: a duplicate, too early, or too late
The packet did not arrive within the implementation's time window
